title: Where’s the “intelligence explosion”?
gist: In a guest post on Noahpinion, Ramez Naam argues that the data from OpenAI, Anthropic and Epoch shows diminishing returns at every level of AI R&D. On his estimate, current self-improvement gives about 2-3% more research productivity per ECI point, against a 15-19% threshold for self-sustaining recursive self-improvement, a 5-10x gap. He expects rapid but not explosive progress, with capex-intensive scaling becoming harder to sustain.

themes.theme: RSI loop too weak for takeoff

insights.claim: Based on current data, the AI self-improvement loop would have to be about 5-10x stronger just to sustain itself, so a sudden explosion to superintelligence is not likely soon, although AI progress will stay very fast by any other technology's standards.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Undercuts fast-takeoff valuation narratives while supporting steady AI growth assumptions.
insights.quote: Given our best current data, the AI self-improvement loop would need to be roughly 5–10× stronger to sustain itself, let alone run away.

insights.claim: Cunningham and colleagues' model puts the threshold for self-sustaining RSI at about 15% more research productivity per extra ECI point, or about 19% after updating with Stockfish data, and their own estimate of current gains is about 9% per point.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Gives a measurable threshold to track for takeoff risk.
insights.locator: In a recent paper, The Economics

insights.claim: OpenAI's logged data shows about 1.6x more experiments per researcher against roughly 16 points of frontier ECI gain, which implies only about 3% productivity gain per ECI point; allowing for extra tokens and compute, Naam uses 2-3%.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: The self-improvement multiplier looks much weaker than survey-based estimates.
insights.quote: I use 2–3% productivity gain per ECI point as a working assumption
insights.locator: Now let’s use OpenAI’s experiment data

insights.claim: OpenAI's logged experiments are a better measure than Anthropic's opt-in survey of 130 staff (which reported about 4x productivity) because they are directly measured, cover everyone, and are far larger.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Investors should prefer logged metrics over self-reported AI productivity claims.

insights.claim: Naam's taxonomy has five types of RSI: productivity gains (Type 1), growing autonomy that still faces diminishing returns (Types 2-4), and runaway superintelligence (Type 5). Types 1-2 have been achieved, Type 3 lacks clear evidence (despite Alibaba's claims), and Type 4 has not been seen.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Gives a way to judge lab claims about self-improvement.

insights.claim: Noah Smith, in his intro, is agnostic on takeoff and says the debate may matter little in practice, because AI improving this fast will look godlike by 2040 either way.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Strong AI is expected even without a singularity.
insights.quote: The AI of 2040 is going to look godlike, whether or not it explodes into an actual god in 2027.

insights.claim: Noam Brown says recursive self-improvement, meaning AI doing AI research, is OpenAI's top priority by a wide margin, ranked above making models that sell.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: OpenAI is putting research automation ahead of near-term commercial products.

insights.claim: In OpenAI's internal research data, the task length its models could complete autonomously with 80% success was about 15 minutes, and even on tasks under 15 minutes they succeeded without help only 86% of the time.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Autonomous AI research is far less mature than benchmarks suggest.
insights.quote: Even on tasks that would take a human less than 15 minutes, OpenAI’s models succeeded without human intervention only 86% of the time.
insights.locator: In its Research Acceleration / RSI report

insights.claim: A 4-hour benchmark horizon (ECI-extrapolated METR) is about 16x OpenAI's real research horizon, and AI 2027's 11-hour forecast is about 44x, so real AI research is an order of magnitude or more harder than benchmarks and forecasts show.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Forecasts like AI 2027 look over-optimistic, so be cautious about timelines priced off benchmarks.
insights.quote: Actual AI research at OpenAI is an order of magnitude or more harder than metrics, benchmarks, or forecasts suggest.

insights.claim: Anthropic's data shows internal models working on or leading more than 90% of R&D tasks, but zero cases of AI completing AI R&D tasks on its own.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: AI is a strong research assistant but still needs humans to direct it.

insights.claim: METR estimated Mythos Preview succeeds at 80% of coding tasks that take humans three hours, and Epoch's rule of thumb is that 5 ECI points roughly double the METR horizon.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Gives benchmark points for tracking capability progress.
insights.locator: For years, METR has been publishing

insights.claim: Narrow superintelligence already exists in highly verifiable domains such as chess, Go, formal math and parts of coding, shown by OpenAI's AI-generated Navier-Stokes proof, but it does not carry over to broad superintelligence.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Expect superhuman AI first in math, coding and cybersecurity, not in open-ended judgment work.

insights.claim: Opus 5.5 gains only 2.6 points on CoBench, Anthropic's benchmark built from historical AI R&D problems, which is within error bars, while it improves a lot on coding and computer-use benchmarks.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Gains in AI research ability lag gains on general benchmarks.

insights.claim: Anthropic says Opus 5.5 is weaker at open-ended research, mostly testing incremental ideas, and METR expects full automation of AI R&D to need big gains in research 'judgement' or 'taste'.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Research taste is the bottleneck to watch for a takeoff signal.
insights.quote: internal users report that it mostly tests incremental ideas and prefers less ambitious hypotheses
insights.locator: AI Still Struggles With Big Research Ideas

insights.claim: At OpenAI, researchers used 124x more tokens per person and engineers shipped about 7x more code, yet experiments per researcher rose only 1.6x over the 2025 average.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Huge token use turns into modest research output, a warning on token-demand-based productivity stories.
insights.quote: Researchers used 124x more tokens per person.

insights.claim: Anthropic's Mythos Preview system card estimates staff productivity uplift of about 4x (geometric mean), and says doubling overall progress would take roughly an order of magnitude more uplift, about 40x versus no AI.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Productivity gains do not translate one-for-one into capability gains.
insights.quote: Productivity uplift does not translate one-for-one to capabilities progress.

insights.claim: Because science has steep diminishing returns to experiments, a 60% rise in experiment pace may mean only about a 10% boost in AI improvement pace (power-law exponent 0.2).
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Higher research throughput may barely speed up capability gains.
insights.locator: We don’t yet know how much

insights.claim: Test-time compute shows logarithmic returns: each doubling of compute gives about the same gain in success rate at twice the cost.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Inference-heavy reasoning gets costly fast, which matters for compute demand and margins.
insights.locator: Test Time Compute Also Has Diminishing Returns

insights.claim: Toby Ord's rule of thumb is that agent-swarm speedup scales with the square root of agent count, so 100 agents finish a task 10x faster at 10x the token cost; AI agents also lack diversity, with each pair of extra AI responses adding about one human's worth of creativity.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Swarms trade money for speed, which helps cyber offense but less so research breakthroughs.

insights.claim: Swarms can still be dangerous even when inefficient, such as for finding cyber vulnerabilities, where speed justifies huge token costs.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Cyber is the area where AI swarms create risk soonest.
insights.quote: Swarms can be dangerous even when they’re inefficient.
insights.locator: I do think Lisan makes good points

insights.claim: Noam Brown credits multi-agent methods with less than 10% of OpenAI's Navier-Stokes result; most of it came from a better model built with large-scale RL.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Better models matter more than running more copies.
insights.locator: OpenAI’s Noam Brown made the central point

insights.claim: Data, compute, model size and RL compute all show diminishing returns in published scaling studies, and these power laws go back to Cortes et al. in 1993.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Each capability step will keep getting more expensive.

insights.claim: Epoch estimates returns to research effort on Stockfish at about 0.83, and in a Karpathy autoresearch run about 92% of the gains came within 44 of 89 experiments.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Automated research also hits diminishing returns early.

insights.claim: Research productivity falls across fields as effort grows (Bloom et al.); under Eroom's Law, the inflation-adjusted R&D cost per approved drug roughly doubled every nine years.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: The 'ideas get harder to find' problem is a structural headwind for AI R&D too.
insights.locator: This pattern shows up across R&D.

insights.claim: The frontier ECI score has risen about 16 points a year from January 2024 to September 2026, which is fast but shows no runaway acceleration, and the apparent trend break in Anthropic's data looks like a one-time jump.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Capability trends point to steady linear gains, not exponential surprises.
insights.quote: What looked like acceleration now appears more consistent with a one-time jump.
insights.locator: The public ECI frontier-the best score

insights.claim: Epoch estimates AI chip capacity (in H100 equivalents) grew about 127x in just over three years while measured capability grew steadily, so ever more inputs are needed to keep gains going.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Capability is buying much less per unit of compute, so capex efficiency is falling.

insights.claim: AI infrastructure now takes about 3% of U.S. GDP and can no longer be paid for from hyperscaler profits, so future spending depends on AI revenue; investment growth will likely slow from its exponential pace and capability progress may slow with it.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: A key risk for AI capex and semis: if revenue lags, growth in investment and capability both slow.
insights.quote: 3% of US GDP is now going into AI infrastructure
insights.locator: We’ve been able to scale these inputs

insights.claim: Anthropic says internal AI use has been key to maintaining the current rate of progress, with no clear sign of dramatic acceleration, which suggests better AI may be needed just to keep pace.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: AI tools are offsetting harder problems rather than speeding up progress.
insights.quote: we believe that internal usage of recent AI models has been a key factor in maintaining the current rate of progress

insights.claim: A Transformer-scale breakthrough, better training data, memory or research judgment, or combined software-hardware-economic feedback loops (Davidson, Halperin, Houlden, Korinek) could overcome the weak software loop and justify revisiting these estimates.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: These are the signals that would invalidate the slow-takeoff view.

insights.claim: Naam doubts the Davidson et al. calibration that puts a fully automated software loop at the explosive threshold, and notes it leaves out the years of lag in turning chip designs into deployed hardware.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Physical lags in chips and data centers cap how fast takeoff could happen.
insights.locator: On hardware, I have some further

insights.claim: Labs should disclose more RSI metrics, such as useful research added per model at fixed resources, along the lines of the Elasticity Institute's eight-point 'How to Measure RSI' proposal.
insights.speaker: Ramez Naam
insights.so_what: Better disclosure would let investors track takeoff risk directly.
